growth_story.headline: Canada's income per person has grown 1.0 percent a year since 1990, slowing to 0.5 in the last decade as productivity lagged and population surged.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, Canada's income per person has grown at a steady average of 1.0 percent a year with no lasting change of pace: the data show one long era, broken by short recessions. Income per person fell 3.3 percent in the early-1990s recession of 1991, then grew 4.3 percent in 1999 and 4.2 in 2000. The 2009 global crisis cut it by 4.0 percent, but the IMF describes a rapid recovery, with a financial system that kept lending through the crisis. Growth then eased, from 0.6 percent a year over 2006-2015 to 0.5 over 2016-2025, as the oil price collapse that began in 2014 hit investment and as productivity kept trailing other rich economies. After a 6.1 percent fall in the 2020 pandemic and a rebound, income per person peaked in 2022, then fell in 2023 and 2024 while the population grew very fast through immigration. Higher U.S. tariffs added a new shock in 2025: income per person grew 0.8 percent that year, but it is still 1.0 percent below its 2022 peak and about where it first was in 2018.

threads.title: Productivity trailing other rich economies
threads.text: Sources describe productivity growth that has trailed the best-performing rich economies for many years, with low investment and low business research spending. The IMF says the 2025 trade shock reinforced these long-standing weaknesses.

threads.title: A population surge from immigration
threads.text: Canada's population grew very fast in 2023 and 2024. More people added to the workforce, but this further strained already weak productivity, and income per person fell in both years. The IMF lists slowing immigration among the drags on growth in 2025.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Canada 2025

threads.title: The U.S. tariff shock
threads.text: Higher U.S. tariffs in 2025 disrupted supply chains closely tied to the United States, the largest change in North American trade policy since NAFTA. Uncertainty about trade weighed on exports, investment and confidence.

threads.title: The oil price collapse
threads.text: Oil is a major export, and it lost more than half its value from 2014, which brought a slump in business investment. Income per person slipped 0.1 percent in both 2015 and 2016.

threads.text: In the 2009 global crisis, Canada's financial system kept lending and the economy came out of the crisis quickly. The 2020 pandemic brought the deepest fall since 1990, 6.1 percent, which was met by fast policy action and followed by a 5.4 percent rebound in 2021.

growth_story.tension: The OECD calls the economy resilient, with growth picking up over 2024, yet income per person fell 1.0 percent in 2024 after a 0.8 percent fall in 2023. Total output grew, but the population grew faster, so the pickup the sources describe does not show up per person; the OECD itself notes that per capita performance has lagged.
